claims.claim: A new Muslim makes ghusl in the first day or two (stated as advice, no ruling given)
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search-result excerpts), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/81949/when-is-ghusl-required-and-when-is-it-mustahabb and https://islamqa.info/en/answers/975/causes-that-make-ghusl-a-must: 'The Malikis and Hanbalis are of the view that if a disbeliever becomes Muslim, ghusl is required ... The Hanafis and Shafi'is are of the view that it is encouraged'; 'If a disbeliever becomes Muslim when he is in the state of janabah, then he has to do ghusl.'

claims.claim: The Prophet told converts to make ghusl (basis of the practice)
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/abudawud:355: Qays ibn Asim came to the Prophet intending to embrace Islam and was commanded to take a bath with water and lote-tree leaves; also in Tirmidhi and Nasa'i.

claims.claim: Ghusl on conversion is recommended, obligatory if in a state of major ritual impurity before praying
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/islamic-belief/is-ghusl-required-after-saying-the-shahada-shaykh-abdul-rahim-reasat/: 'it is recommended that they perform a ritual bath'; 'only obligatory for the one who just enters Islam if they are in a state of major ritual impurity and are going to perform the prayers'.

rows.notes: Ghusl advice is consistent with the sources. The schools differ: Maliki and Hanbali say obligatory on conversion, Hanafi and Shafi'i say recommended unless the person was in a state of major impurity, in which case all agree it is needed before prayer. The description does not need to choose, but it could say 'before your first prayer'.
rows.method: 3 web searches (islamqa.info, sunnah.com, seekersguidance.org search-result excerpts); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Zakat becomes an obligation once its conditions (the nisab threshold) apply
claims.evidence: IslamQA, https://islamqa.info/en/answers/99381: if wealth falls short of the nisab, no zakah is due, and if it drops below the nisab during the year no zakah is due; https://islamqa.info/en/64: the nisab is 85 g of gold or 595 g of silver, the rate 2.5%, after one full lunar year.

rows.notes: Both statements are the standard Sunni position. Zakat also needs a full lunar year (hawl) on the wealth, which 'once the conditions apply' covers. Sending the reader to someone qualified is the right framing.

claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): all four Sunni schools hold that deliberate ejaculation from kissing or touching breaks the fast; they differ only on whether expiation is also due (Maliki: yes). claims.claim: The Prophet recommended breaking the fast with dates and water
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): Sunan Abi Dawud 2356 (Anas): fresh dates, else dried dates, else sips of water; Sunan Abi Dawud 2355 and Tirmidhi 658 (Salman ibn Amir): break with dates, if not, water, for it is pure; https://sunnah.com/abudawud:2356. The step gives no hadith id for this.

claims.claim: Each day's fast needs a fresh intention (niyyah)
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): this is the Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali position; the Maliki school holds that one intention at the start of Ramadan covers the whole month if the fast is not interrupted. Stated as agreed.

rows.notes: Two scope problems: 'in the Hanafi school' marks a point all four schools agree on, so a non-Hanafi reader may think it does not break their fast; the daily-intention rule is stated as agreed although the Maliki school accepts one intention for the month. Add a hadith id for dates and water (Abu Dawud 2356). Suhoor line is fine (Bukhari 1923).
rows.method: Compared with standard fiqh references and the step's cited SeekersGuidance (Hanafi) source note; not confirmed online (the automated search quota was used up, direct page opening was not available).

claims.claim: Pilgrims wear plain white garments (ihram)

claims.claim: Hajj ends with Eid al-Adha
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search-result excerpts), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/66193 and /36436: Eid al-Adha is the 10th of Dhul Hijjah and the days of al-Tashreeq (11th to 13th) follow it, with the stoning continuing and the farewell tawaf required before leaving; so Eid falls on the third day of Hajj and the rites run two or three days beyond it

rows.notes: Two statements need rewording: (1) the white garments are the men's ihram; women wear ordinary modest clothing in any colour, so say 'men wear two plain white cloths and women ordinary modest dress'; (2) Eid al-Adha (10 Dhul Hijjah) falls during Hajj, and the rites continue through the 12th or 13th, so say 'Eid al-Adha falls during Hajj' rather than 'Hajj ends with' it.

claims.claim: Many Canadian masjids are registered charities or non-profits run by an elected volunteer board that employs the imam
claims.evidence: Secondary sources (search-result excerpts): charitylawgroup.ca 'Guidance to Registering a Mosque, Church and Temple as a Canadian Charity' (mosques registering as charities must form a board of directors or trustees); orghub.ca 'Annual General Meetings for Canadian Charities' (directors must hold an annual members' meeting where members elect directors and receive financial statements); iqra.ca 'Overcoming Power Imbalances on Mosque Boards' (board disputes can end with an imam dismissed). claims.claim: The CRA List of charities shows registration status, contact information, general activities and financial information
claims.evidence: Canada.ca (search-result excerpt), https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/charities-giving/charities/information-about-a-charity.html: 'The List of charities provides a registered charity's registration status, contact information, general activities, and financial information' (from the T3010 returns for the last five fiscal periods).

rows.notes: Both CRA statements match canada.ca. The governance description rests on general secondary sources and is suitably hedged. Precision point: the CRA page frames what it handles as non-compliance with the Income Tax Act; 'does not handle everyday disputes' is a fair reading but not a quoted line.

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 305: 'This is the thing which Allah has ordained for all the daughters of Adam' (Aisha's period on Hajj)
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:305: 'We set out with the Prophet for Hajj and when we reached Sarif I got my menses... This is the thing which Allah has ordained for all the daughters of Adam'; he told her to do all the rites except tawaf.

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 297: the Prophet leaned on Aisha's lap and recited Quran while she was menstruating
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:297: the Prophet 'used to lean on my lap and recite Qur'an while I was in menses' (chapter on reciting in the lap of one's menstruating wife).

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 298a: 'Your menstruation is not in your hand' (fetching the mat from the mosque)
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/muslim:298a: 'Get me the mat from the mosque. She said: I am menstruating. Upon this he remarked: Your menstruation is not in your hand.'

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 335c and Sahih al-Bukhari 321: missed fasts are made up, missed prayers are not; Bukhari 305: every Hajj rite except tawaf
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpts), https://sunnah.com/muslim:335c: 'we were ordered to complete the fasts, but were not ordered to complete the prayers'; https://sunnah.com/bukhari:321: 'he never ordered us to offer them (the prayers missed during menses)'; https://sunnah.com/bukhari:305: 'perform all the ceremonies of Hajj like the others, but do not perform the Tawaf'.

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 302: 'Do everything except intercourse', and the Prophet's displeasure at cutting women off during their periods
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/muslim:302: the Jews would not eat with or live with a menstruating woman; the Prophet said 'Do everything except intercourse'; his face changed when two companions asked whether to do as the Jews did.

claims.claim: Sunan Abi Dawud 212 ('what is above the waist-wrapper is lawful') and Sahih al-Bukhari 302 (izar during menses) as the basis of the barrier view
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpts), https://sunnah.com/abudawud:212: 'What is above the waist-wrapper is lawful for you'; https://sunnah.com/bukhari:302: 'he used to order her to put on an Izar' before fondling during her period.

claims.claim: Hanafi, Maliki and Shafi'i schools ask for a barrier between navel and knee; the Hanbali school allows everything except intercourse
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search-result excerpt), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/36722: 'Imam Abu Hanifah, Imam Malik and al-Shafi'i were of the view that intimacy between the navel and the knee is haram, and Imam Ahmad was of the view that this is permissible'. SeekersGuidance (Hanafi, Yusuf Weltch), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/halal-and-haram/what-type-of-intimacy-is-permitted-between-a-husband-and-a-wife-during-her-menstruation/: 'Any contact between the navel and the knees must be done over a barrier... skin-to-skin contact anywhere else on her body is permissible.'

rows.notes: All hadith citations and the four-school summary match the sources. The site's own sources.json note says its SeekersGuidance answer covers the Hanafi view only; IslamQA 36722 supplies the school-by-school attribution and could be added as a source. The prayer-owed timing point is kept general, which is fine.
rows.method: 7 web searches (sunnah.com, islamqa.info, seekersguidance.org); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 324: menstruating women come out for Eid and the gathering of believers but keep away from the musalla
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:324 (Umm Atiyya): 'the menstruating women should come out and participate in the good deeds as well as the religious gathering of the faithful believers but the menstruating women should keep away from the Musalla'.

claims.claim: Hanafi and Shafi'i scholars (SeekersGuidance answers) list dua, dhikr, salawat, listening to Quran, charity and learning as open during menses
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/what-are-acts-of-worship-a-menstruating-woman-can-engage-in/: dhikr ('recommended in the Hanafi school for women in their periods to sit making dhikr in the place they normally pray'), dua, Quranic verses said with the intention of supplication, and listening to the Quran 'while pondering its deep meanings'; a Shafi'i counterpart 'Can a Woman Do These Acts of Worship during Her Menses?' is listed on the same site.

rows.notes: Bukhari 324 matches and the list of acts that carry on matches the cited SeekersGuidance answers; these points are agreed across the schools.
rows.method: 2 web searches (sunnah.com, seekersguidance.org); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Hanafi and Shafi'i schools: no Quran recitation during menses; listening, looking and Quranic phrases as dua or dhikr are allowed
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (Shafi'i, search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity-shafii-fiqh/can-a-menstruating-woman-read-and-touch-the-quran/: reciting is 'permissible if it is with the intention of remembrance, and not with the intention of Quran recitation' (Khatib Shirbini); the Hanafi answer on acts of worship gives the same dua and dhikr exception.

claims.claim: Maliki school: recitation is allowed while the bleeding continues
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/a-menstruating-woman-reciting-the-quran-the-maliki-position-sticking-to-one-school-and-the-path-of-taqwa/: 'the Maliki School permits reciting the Quran for the menstruating woman while her bleeding is continuous, unconditionally', and permits touching the mushaf for those learning or teaching.

claims.claim: IslamQA and an AMJA scholar allow reciting from memory; the AMJA answer allows touching the mushaf when needed and says a phone or tablet app is not a mushaf
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search-result excerpt), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/2564: 'permissible for a menstruating woman to recite the Quran from memory, not from the Mus-haf'. AMJA fatwa 86681 (search-result excerpt), https://www.amjaonline.org/fatwa/en/86681/question-about-reading-divine-text-while-in-menstruation: reciting during menstruation 'is counted and accepted'; 'Some scholars allowed touching the mushaf for menstruating women if there is a need'; 'an electronic device with the Qur'an on it, will not take the same ruling as a mushaf'.

claims.claim: Touching a printed mushaf: most scholars say not to; some allow it with a covering; the Hanafi school is careful about printed translations and tafsir
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance Shafi'i answer (search-result excerpt): 'The majority of scholars among the Companions, Followers, and the Imams of the four schools have agreed on the prohibition of a menstruating woman touching the Mushaf'; IslamQA 2564: 'forbidden to touch the mus-haf'. The covered-hand allowance and the Hanafi caution on translations were not shown in the search-result excerpts (standard references, not confirmed online).

rows.notes: The positions are stated accurately and attributed correctly; the section rightly declines to choose. Two lesser points were not visible in the search-result excerpts: the allowance to touch the mushaf through a covering (a Hanafi and Hanbali view) and the Hanafi caution about printed translations and tafsir.
rows.method: 5 web searches (seekersguidance.org x2, islamqa.info, amjaonline.org); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Most schools say not to stay in the prayer hall during menses and differ on passing through
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search-result excerpts), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/33649 and https://islamqa.info/en/answers/60213: 'The majority of jurists of the four Schools of Fiqh are of the view that it is not permissible for a menstruating woman to enter and stay in the mosque'; 'simply passing through is allowed, if she needs to and she is certain that she will not make the mosque impure'. The Hanafi answer below bars entry altogether, so the schools do differ on passing through.

claims.claim: Classrooms, halls and offices may not count as the masjid; ask which rooms count (Hanafi answer on a hifz class)
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/can-a-menstruating-woman-enter-the-masjid-for-a-hifz-class/: in the Hanafi school a menstruating woman does not enter the masjid, 'and this applies to any area directly above and below what has been designated as a masjid', but 'if there is a part of the building which was excluded from being classed as a mosque... then she can enter that area'; it suggests holding the class in a separate classroom.

rows.notes: Both statements match the cited Hanafi answer and IslamQA's four-school summary. The advice to ask which rooms count as the masjid follows the Hanafi answer closely.
rows.method: 2 web searches (seekersguidance.org, islamqa.info); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 306: the Prophet told Fatima bint Abi Hubaish to leave prayer during her period, then wash and pray
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:306: 'I do not become clean (from bleeding). Shall I give up my prayers? ... No, because it is from a blood vessel and not the menses'; the hadith continues with leaving prayer for the period, then washing and praying.

claims.claim: A period ends with white discharge or complete dryness; the schools differ on these signs and on brown or yellow discharge
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search-result excerpt), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/317771: 'There are two signs of the end of the period: dryness and the white discharge'; most jurists accept dryness 'except for what was narrated from Imam Malik'; brownish or yellowish discharge after the end of menses 'is not menses' (Umm Atiyyah). SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity/what-is-the-difference-between-menstruation-and-istihada/: check with 'a piece of white cotton or tissue' and keep a record.

rows.notes: Bukhari 306 matches, and the end-of-period signs match IslamQA and the cited SeekersGuidance answer, including the note that the schools differ. 'Full-body wash' follows the site's ghusl wording rule.
rows.method: 3 web searches (sunnah.com, islamqa.info, seekersguidance.org); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 306: istihadah does not stop prayer; leave prayer only during the real period, then wash and pray
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:306: 'No, because it is from a blood vessel and not the menses' (Fatima bint Abi Hubaish).

claims.claim: Hanafi excused person: bleeding so constant that there is no time for wudu and a short obligatory prayer; one wudu per prayer time, lasting until the time ends
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity/what-is-the-ruling-regarding-excused-person/ and related answers: one is excused 'only if the issue... lasts for an entire prayer time, such that there is not enough of a gap of time to perform a valid wudu and prayer'; the wudu 'is vitiated by the exiting of the prayer time'.

claims.claim: Other schools use different day limits to sort a period from other bleeding
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity/what-is-the-difference-between-menstruation-and-istihada/: in the Shafi'i school blood 'beyond 15 days after your last period ended' is menstruation, less than 15 days is istihada; the Hanafi maximum period is 10 days (standard references).

rows.notes: All three points match the cited SeekersGuidance answers and Sunnah.com. The excused-person summary is a fair simplification of the Hanafi rule, and the text rightly sends readers to a doctor and a teacher.
rows.method: 3 web searches (sunnah.com, seekersguidance.org x2); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Nifas follows the rules of a period: no prayer or fasting, make up the fasts but not the prayers; ghusl and pray when it stops
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search-result excerpt), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/319: 'If the woman sees that she is pure, which is when the bleeding stops, then she should do ghusl and start praying'; the make-up rule rests on Sahih Muslim 335c and Bukhari 321 (confirmed under R0477) and nifas is treated like hayd in all schools (standard references).

claims.claim: The schools set the longest length of nifas differently
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search-result excerpt), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/319: forty days is 'the view of Abu Haneefah and Ahmad'; 'Maalik, al-Shaafa'i and Ahmad, according to one report, said that the longest it may last is 60 days'; 'Most of the scholars have not set any limit for the minimum'. The topic's cited Sunan Abi Dawud 311 (Umm Salamah: 'would refrain (from prayer) for forty days or forty nights') was confirmed in a GitHub mirror of sunnah.com data, and Sunnah.com surfaced the parallel https://sunnah.com/abudawud:312.

rows.notes: The statements match IslamQA's summary of the schools and are phrased carefully. Lesser point: the grade the site's source note gives Abu Dawud 311 (Hasan Sahih, al-Albani) was not visible in the search-result excerpts. Medical advice is kept separate from the religious guidance.
rows.method: 2 web searches (islamqa.info, sunnah.com) plus a GitHub mirror check for Abu Dawud 311; direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Men's awrah is navel to knee, knee included (Hanafi answer on SeekersGuidance), covered at all times unless there is a need; the swimming answer says a little past the knee with three-quarter compression pants
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpts), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/what-is-considered-awra-nakedness-for-men/: 'from the end of the navel down to, and including the knee... covered at all times unless there is a need'; https://seekersguidance.org/answers/general-counsel/covering-nakedness-while-swimming/: 'obligatory to cover between navel and knees, and a little beyond' and 'three quarter length compression pants to wear under your regular swimming shorts'.

claims.claim: Men do not wear gold or silk
claims.evidence: Sunan an-Nasa'i 5148 confirmed in a GitHub mirror of sunnah.com data (fawazahmed0/wiki-test): 'Gold and silk have been permitted for the females of my Ummah, and forbidden to the males', graded Sahih (Al-Albani); site-cited URL https://sunnah.com/nasai:5148 not reached directly.

claims.claim: Women cover everything except the face and hands before non-mahram men; Quran 24:31 head coverings over the chest, 33:59 outer garments; both sexes lower the gaze (24:30-31)
claims.evidence: Quran.com (search-result excerpts), https://quran.com/an-nur/31: 'tell the believing women to lower their gaze... Let them draw their veils over their chests'; https://quran.com/al-ahzab/59: 'draw their cloaks over their bodies... recognized as virtuous and not be harassed'. SeekersGuidance (Hanafi), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/a-detailed-exposition-of-the-fiqh-of-covering-ones-nakedness-awra/: a free woman's awra is 'her full body... except for the face, hands, and feet', with covering the feet advised as caution.

claims.claim: The women's swimming answer asks for loose clothing that is not thin
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/modesty/is-swimming-permissible-for-women-in-islam/: 'obligatory to cover oneself with loose, modest, and non-transparent clothing', women-only settings, and a married woman seeks her husband's permission.

rows.notes: All points match the cited answers and verses. Two notes: the gold-and-silk hadith was confirmed only through a mirror of sunnah.com data, and the Hanafi awrah answer leaves out the feet as well as the face and hands, while the site says 'except the face and hands' (the majority view); the site's 'schools differ on smaller details' covers this.

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 261a lists ten acts of the fitrah including those named; Sahih Muslim 258 sets a forty-night limit
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpts), https://sunnah.com/muslim:261a: 'Ten are the acts according to fitra: clipping the moustache, letting the beard grow, using the tooth-stick, snuffing water in the nose, cutting the nails, washing the finger joints, plucking the hair under the armpits, shaving the pubes and cleaning one's private parts with water' (the narrator forgot the tenth, perhaps rinsing the mouth); https://sunnah.com/muslim:258: 'clipping the moustache, cutting the nails, plucking hair under the armpits, shaving the pubes... not be neglected far more than forty nights'.

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 5892: keep the beards and cut the moustaches short; Ibn Umar cut what went past his fist
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5892: 'Do the opposite of what the pagans do. Keep the beards and cut the moustaches short'; whenever Ibn Umar performed Hajj or Umra he held his beard and cut whatever remained outside his hold.

claims.claim: SeekersGuidance: Hanafi wajib at a fist and shaving prohibited, Maliki unlawful (al-Dasuqi); Shafi'i relied-upon view recommended, shaving disliked not forbidden, majority hold shaving unlawful, all agree it is blameworthy
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpts), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/what-is-a-beard-in-the-hanafi-school/: 'In the Hanafi school, it is wajib for the beard to be a fistful'; 'according to Dasuqi... It is unlawful (haram) for a man to shave off his beard'; https://seekersguidance.org/answers/shafii-fiqh/ruling-shaving-shortening-beard-shafii-school/: al-Rafi'i and al-Nawawi 'ruled that to keep a full beard is merely recommended', shaving or shortening is 'disliked' and 'not sinful'. The 'majority' and 'blameworthy' lines were not shown in the search-result excerpt.

claims.claim: Ontario's creed policy (section 10.2) says dress and appearance rules must accommodate a religious beard short of undue hardship, with a bearded Sikh security guard as the example
claims.evidence: OHRC (search-result excerpt), https://www.ohrc.on.ca/en/policy-preventing-discrimination-based-creed/10-specific-cases: rules 'requiring no beards or head coverings... may come into direct conflict with religious requirements. When they do, there is a duty to accommodate the person, short of undue hardship'; a security company's policy 'requiring all security guards to wear a hat and be clean-shaven was found to have discriminated against a turbaned Sikh man'. The sub-section number 10.2 was not visible in the search-result excerpt.

rows.notes: The three hadith, both SeekersGuidance beard answers and the OHRC example all match. Minor: the Shafi'i answer's 'majority' and 'blameworthy' lines and the OHRC sub-section number were not visible in search-result excerpts, and the claim that the fitrah list applies to women apart from beard and moustache is standard but carries no citation.

claims.claim: Five obligatory prayers with 2, 4, 4, 3 and 4 rak'ahs
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/number-cycle-obligatory-prayers/: 'The obligatory cycles (rak'ahs) are seventeen: two at Fajr, four at Zuhr, Asr and Isha, and three at Maghrib'; agreed by all schools.

claims.claim: Time windows: Fajr before sunrise, Dhuhr after the sun passes its highest point, Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib after sunset, Isha once twilight is gone
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/muslim:612a (and 612d): 'The time of the noon prayer is when the sun passes the meridian... the time for the afternoon prayer is as long as the sun has not become pale. The time of the evening prayer is as long as the twilight has not ended. The time of the night prayer is up to the middle of the average night, and the time of the morning prayer is from the appearance of dawn, as long as the sun has not risen.'

rows.notes: The windows match Sahih Muslim 612 and the rak'ah counts match SeekersGuidance. Precision point: 'anywhere inside its window' is broadly true, though the schools dislike delaying Asr until the sun yellows and Isha past midnight.

claims.claim: Bukhari 1147: the Prophet's night prayer never exceeded eleven rak'ahs in Ramadan or otherwise; Bukhari 1129: he led night prayer in Ramadan a few nights then stopped for fear it would be made obligatory; Muslim 720 (duha); Bukhari 444 (two rak'ahs on entering a masjid)

claims.claim: The Maliki summary lists two before Fajr, four before and after Dhuhr, four before Asr, two or more after Maghrib, nothing set after Friday prayer; the Hanafi text lists four before and four after Friday prayer

claims.claim: Shafi'i combining: in the time of the first prayer, with order, intention during the first prayer and continuity
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/shafii-fiqh/considered-traveller-shafii/: to combine 'you must have done three things: prayed in order; intended to combine prayers at some point during the first prayer; and prayed the second prayer after the first prayer without a long break between the two'.

claims.claim: Hanafi: real combining only at Arafah and Muzdalifah; praying at the end of one time and the start of the next is allowed; a Hanafi may follow another school's combining if all its conditions are met
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/combining-prayers-hanafi-school-possible/: 'not valid to combine Zuhr with Asr, nor Maghrib with Isha unless one is in a state of Ihram at Arafat and Muzdalifa'; other combination 'is only superficial: one delays the first prayer to just before the end of its time'; following another school is possible but 'blending between madhabs in a manner which would render the action impermissible in any one of them is not allowed'.

claims.claim: AMJA keeps only witr and the two before Fajr on a journey; the Hanafi answer keeps sunnah prayers unless in the rush of travel; the Hanafi plane answer: stand, bow and prostrate if possible, otherwise repeat a prayer prayed seated with head movements
claims.evidence: AMJA fatwa 3078 (search-result excerpt): the Prophet 'did not quit praying, even while traveling, Sunnat Al-Fajr and Salatu Al-Witr'. SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpts), Hanafi travel answer: 'One still prays the sunna prayers though, unless in the midst of a journey and in the rush of travel'; https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/can-i-pray-on-a-plane/: 'obligatory on an airplane to pray standing with bowing and prostration'; with head movements only, 'the prayer would have to be repeated once you arrive at your destination'; praying when the time enters in flight is valid.

rows.notes: Both general statements hold. Under BC's statute, with no named personal representative the burial decision passes to the spouse, then adult children, so a convert's non-Muslim next of kin may decide. The page correctly says it is not legal advice.

claims.claim: Ontario: a dependant (spouse, former spouse, child, parent, sibling) can claim support from the estate, usually within 6 months of the estate trustee being named
claims.evidence: Steps to Justice (search-result excerpt), https://stepstojustice.ca/steps/wills-and-powers-of-attorney/1-think-about-making-a-dependants-support-claim/: 'within 6 months of a person being named the estate trustee ... claims.claim: Ontario: a married spouse chooses between the will and an equalization payment and must ask the court within 6 months of the death

rows.notes: Both routes and both six-month rules confirmed against the cited pages and the statutes. 'Usually' is right because the court can allow a late dependant claim against undistributed assets and can extend the equalization deadline.

claims.claim: Kosher meat: the Hanafi and Hanbali schools require God's name over each animal; the Shafi'i school treats it as recommended

claims.claim: A Hanafi answer calls catch-and-release fishing impermissible
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/fiqh-answers-2/what-is-the-ruling-of-catch-and-release-fishing-if-it-is-done-to-sharpen-skills-not-for-fun-or-sports/: 'impermissible ... even if it is done to sharpen skills', because it often leads to the death of the fish; alternative is to keep and eat a legal catch. claims.claim: A nikah needs an offer and acceptance, witnesses and a mahr
claims.evidence: IslamQA 111127 'Is Marriage Valid without Mahr?', https://islamqa.info/en/answers/111127: a contract 'without any mention of the mahr ... is valid and the wife is entitled to a mahr like that of her peers'. AMJA Family Code, https://www.amjaonline.org/declaration-articles/the-assemblys-family-code-for-muslim-communities-in-north-america: 'specifying a dowry is not one of its main pillars'. Witnesses and offer/acceptance are conditions (IslamQA 159297).

claims.claim: Three of the four schools also require a wali for the bride
claims.evidence: IslamQA 254835, https://islamqa.info/en/answers/254835: 'The guardian is a condition of marriage being valid according to the majority of scholars'; 'the Hanafis ... regard it permissible to get married without a guardian' with two witnesses. AMJA fatwa 87635, https://www.amjaonline.org/fatwa/en/87635/marriage-when-bride-has-no-wali-guardian: 'valid according to Imam Abu Hanifah ... the other major schools' require the guardian.

claims.claim: A masjid certificate alone is not a legal marriage; a provincial licence and a registered officiant are needed
claims.evidence: Ontario Marriage Act R.S.O. 1990 c. M.3 (e-Laws mirror github.com/hordruma/elaws_scraper; official https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90m03): s.4 licence or banns; s.20 registered officiant; s.25 two witnesses; s.28 signed register. BC Marriage Act ss.7-9, 25 (bclaws mirror); Alberta.ca 'Getting married'; Educaloi Quebec page: authorised officiant, two witnesses, 20-day notice.

claims.claim: Big weddings, gold and engagement parties are custom, not requirements
claims.evidence: general statement; consistent with Bukhari 5167 ('a banquet, even if with one sheep') and AMJA's 'no minimum mahr'

rows.notes: One precision point: the mahr is the wife's right and is due in every marriage, but it is not a condition of the contract's validity; IslamQA and AMJA both say a contract that does not mention the mahr is valid and a customary mahr becomes due. 'Needs' is a fair simplification for a summary if the section explains it. Wali and legal points hold.

claims.claim: Ontario: licence or banns; religious officiant recognised by their religious body; couple, two witnesses and officiant sign right after; good-faith marriages can be treated as valid
claims.evidence: Ontario Marriage Act R.S.O. 1990 c. M.3, from a GitHub mirror of e-Laws (github.com/hordruma/elaws_scraper, to 31 Dec 2022; official https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90m03): s.4 'licence ... or the publication of banns'; s.20.1(1)(b) officiant 'duly recognized by the religious body'; s.25 'at least two witnesses who shall affix their names'; s.28(1) register signed 'immediately after' by officiant, parties, witnesses; s.31 good-faith marriage 'deemed a valid marriage'.

claims.claim: Quebec: authorised officiant, at least two witnesses, notice published at least 20 days before (Educaloi); BC: officiant registered with Vital Statistics, two witnesses sign; Alberta: registered religious officiants, licence always needed, two witnesses
claims.evidence: Educaloi, https://educaloi.qc.ca/en/capsules/rules-on-marriage-ceremonies-in-quebec/: authorised officiant, 'at least two witnesses', notice 'published on the Directeur's website at least 20 days before'. BC Marriage Act RSBC 1996 c.282 (mirror github.com/boshek/bclaws): s.7(3) registered officiant only; s.9 '2 or more witnesses'; s.25(2) signed by parties, 'at least 2 witnesses', officiant. Alberta.ca https://www.alberta.ca/getting-married: licence; clergy 'registered with Vital Statistics'; 'at least 2 credible witnesses'.

claims.claim: Ontario: married spouses share the value of the family home, common-law partners need not split property; family arbitration under religious law has no legal effect (2006 Act)
claims.evidence: Ontario.ca, https://www.ontario.ca/page/dividing-property-when-marriage-or-common-law-relationship-ends: 'Common law couples are not legally required to split property'; spouses 'must share the full value of the family home'. Family Statute Law Amendment Act, 2006 added Family Law Act s.59.2 (family arbitration only under Ontario or Canadian law), per a 2026 article citing the official consolidation, indexed on GitHub.

claims.claim: Courts in BC and Ontario have enforced mahr agreements and one Ontario court declined (Raman, 2024); AMJA articles 19 and 31
claims.evidence: Raman 2024 confirmed at https://academic.oup.com/lawfam/article/38/1/ebae020/7918419 (IJLPF 38(1)). Kaddoura v Hammoud (1998), https://ca.vlex.com/vid/kaddoura-v-hammoud-681166453: Ontario court held the deferred mahr 'ought not to be enforced'; Khanis v Noormohamed 2011 ONCA 127 enforced one (lawtimesnews.com). AMJA code art. 19 text confirmed at amjaonline.org (arbitrators or community-appointed, state-licensed officiants act for new Muslim women); art. 31 not visible.

rows.notes: Provincial and property rules match the statutes and official pages. Tighten one citation: 'Raman, 2024' is the journal article, not the case; the Ontario court that declined was Kaddoura v Hammoud (1998), and the Ontario Court of Appeal later enforced a mahr in Khanis v Noormohamed (2011), so 'declined' is the older view. AMJA article 31 not confirmable from search-result excerpts; article 19 text confirmed.
rows.method: 6 web searches (educaloi.qc.ca, alberta.ca, ontario.ca, academic.oup.com, case summaries) plus GitHub mirrors of the Ontario and BC Marriage Acts

claims.claim: Above roughly 48.5 degrees of latitude the sun never reaches 18 degrees below the horizon in midsummer

claims.claim: Checked by Shaykh Abdul-Rahim Reasat; fish and vegetarian dishes as a fallback

rows.notes: Matches the SeekersGuidance answer: no obligation to investigate every possible cross-contamination unless a high likelihood is reasonably certain; fried food is the main caution, with fries in shared oil as the example; non-meat options as a fallback. claims.claim: A Hanafi SeekersGuidance answer holds catch-and-release fishing impermissible, even to sharpen skills

claims.claim: 'Keep and eat a legal catch instead' against Canadian rules that require releasing some fish
claims.evidence: Ontario, https://www.ontario.ca/page/fishing-limits-size-restrictions-and-catch-and-release (search-result excerpt): 'You must immediately release any fish that exceed the size restrictions and catch and possession limits'; fish caught out of season or of prohibited size 'must be immediately released'. Legally required release is not the same as sport catch-and-release, but the site's sentence does not say so.

claims.claim: Other SeekersGuidance framing of fishing for sport
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (Hanafi), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/is-fishing-for-sport-permissible/ (search-result excerpt): 'Fishing and hunting for sport are permissible, as long as there is no harm caused to the animal'; a softer framing than the cited hunting answer.

rows.notes: Both SeekersGuidance answers match: hunting for food or income permitted, not for sport; catch-and-release impermissible even to sharpen skills. Two cautions: another SeekersGuidance Hanafi answer allows fishing for sport if the fish is not harmed, and Ontario law requires immediate release of undersized, out-of-season or over-limit fish, so 'keep and eat' needs a legal qualifier.

claims.claim: Shafi'i view (SeekersGuidance, Reliance of the Traveller): a letter mistake spoils that word, which is repeated; the prayer is invalid only if the mistake changes the meaning and was deliberate
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/general-counsel/mispronunciation-of-the-fatiha/: omitting a letter, failing to double one or substituting a wrong letter 'invalidates one's recital of that particular word and one must recite the word again. But it does not invalidate one's prayer unless it changes the meaning and was done deliberately', citing the Reliance as [f18.8].

claims.claim: Hanafi answer citing Ibn Abidin: an accidental saad/seen mix-up does not invalidate the prayer
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/is-my-prayer-valid-if-i-mispronounce-saad-as-seen/: 'Your prayer is valid'; the acted-upon Hanafi position excuses unintentional confusion of letters of close articulation, settled by Ibn Abidin in Radd al-Muhtar on the ground of 'widespread affliction'.

rows.notes: All three sources say what the site says. One numbering point for the source note: the SeekersGuidance page prints the Reliance reference as f18.8, but this passage sits in the Fatiha section of the Reliance (f8.18); f18 is the Friday prayer chapter. Worth writing 'f8.18' with a note, so a reviewer can find it.
rows.method: 3 web searches (sunnah.com for Muslim 798a; seekersguidance.org twice for the two answers); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: SeekersGuidance Hanafi answer (Ibn Abidin): keep or pass on a usable copy; otherwise bury it where no one walks; shredding also allowed
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/how-does-one-dispose-of-an-unused-quran/: 'According to Ibn Abidin, the Qur'an, whether in Arabic or translation, should be buried in a place where no one walks. Scholars have also allowed for shredding', pages shredded beyond recognition or buried in a clean place.

claims.claim: IslamWeb 510508: a damaged cover is no reason to dispose of a copy; unreadable pages may be buried or burned, citing Uthman
claims.evidence: IslamWeb (search-result excerpt), https://islamweb.net/en/fatwa/510508/rulings-related-to-disposal-of-the-mushaf: no need to dispose of a copy while the text is intact and usable; the cover may be replaced; 'If the pages of the Quran are no longer readable, there is no harm in burying or burning them to protect them from desecration', with reference to Uthman's burning of unstandardised manuscripts.

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 4987: Uthman ordered all other Quranic materials burnt after the standard copies were made
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4987 (Virtues of the Qur'an): Uthman sent one copy to every province 'and ordered that all the other Qur'anic materials, whether written in fragmentary manuscripts or whole copies, be burnt.'

rows.notes: Every claim is confirmed in the cited source's own words, and the 'Where opinions differ' box correctly assigns burial and shredding to the Hanafi answer and burning to the IslamWeb fatwa. The recycling-bin line is advice consistent with both. no issues.
rows.method: 3 web searches (sunnah.com for Bukhari 4987; islamweb.net for 510508; seekersguidance.org for the disposal answer); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 223: the Prophet poured water over a milk-fed baby boy's urine and did not wash it
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:223: Umm Qais brought her son who had not started eating ordinary food; he urinated on the Prophet's garment, so he 'asked for water and poured it over the soiled area and did not wash it.'

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 279a: a vessel a dog has licked is washed seven times
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/muslim:279a: 'When a dog licks a utensil belonging to any one of you, the thing contained in it should be thrown away and then the utensil should be washed seven times'; a companion narration (muslim/2/117) adds 'using sand for the first time', which supports the source note that earth appears in another narration.

claims.claim: Shafi'i school (SeekersGuidance, Irshaad Sedick): dog saliva is heavy filth washed seven times, once with earth; light filth is a milk-fed boy's urine, sprinkled; other filth washed until substance, colour and smell are gone
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity-shafii-fiqh/what-distinguishes-the-cleaning-process-between-light-and-moderate-filth/: 'Heavy impurity becomes pure by removing it and then washing it seven times, one of which should be with earth'; 'Light impurity is the urine of a baby (boy), which only feeds on milk and is not yet two years of age', purified by removing it and sprinkling water; all other impurities are moderate.

rows.notes: Both hadith and the Shafi'i answer are confirmed. The general rule 'wash until substance, colour and smell are gone' is the Shafi'i framing for moderate filth; the Hanafi method differs (for example three washes for invisible filth), which the 'Where opinions differ' line covers in general terms. no issues.
rows.method: 2 web searches (sunnah.com for Bukhari 223 and Muslim 279; seekersguidance.org for the Shafi'i filth answer); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Hanafi answer (Sulma Badrudduja): clothes that come out of the washing machine free of any trace of filth may be taken as clean, so no rewash is needed
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/how-do-i-wash-my-clothes-properly-to-ensure-that-filth-doesnt-spread/: 'If one has washed all the clothes together in a washing machine and they come out free of impurities, it would not be necessary to wash each item again'; best to wash the soiled area first.

claims.claim: Hanafi answer (Tabraze Azam): a small mark in underwear found after prayer, absent at wudu, does not require repeating the prayer
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/finding-filth-on-clothing-after-prayer/: 'If you find marks of filth in your undergarments after prayer that was not present before making ablution, you would not repeat your prayers ... Events are ascribed to the nearest possible times.'

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 137 (cited source): do not leave the prayer for an imagined passing of wind unless a sound is heard or a smell noticed
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com search listed https://sunnah.com/bukhari:137 in the Ablutions (Wudu') book; the search-result excerpt did not show its text. The wording (Abbad bin Tamim from his uncle: 'He should not leave his prayer unless he hears sound or smells something') is from standard references, not confirmed online.

rows.notes: Both Hanafi answers say exactly what the site says, and the site rightly labels them Hanafi and narrow. Bukhari 137 exists at the cited number; only its wording was not visible in a search-result excerpt. 'A doubt on its own does not make anything impure' follows the fiqh maxim behind both answers.
rows.method: 2 web searches (seekersguidance.org for both answers; sunnah.com for Bukhari 137, shared with R1277); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Hanafi answer (Faraz Rabbani): alcohol not made from wine is not ritually impure and may be used on the body
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/can-we-use-deodorants-creams-and-perfumes-that-contain-alcohol/: 'Non-wine alcohol is not ritually impure, and as a result, it is permitted in external uses, such as in perfumes and soaps'; deodorants and creams with synthetic alcohol are permitted since it is not khamr.

claims.claim: Avoiding it is more cautious because some scholars, including within the Hanafi school, were stricter
claims.evidence: Same answer (search-result excerpt): 'it is more religiously precautious not to, because of the difference of opinion about it'; a related SG answer notes the later Hanafi fatwa that non-khamr synthetic alcohol is pure, implying earlier stricter views within the school.

rows.notes: The cited answer says what the site says. Precision: the answer defines khamr as alcohol made from grapes and dates, so 'not made from grapes or dates' would be tighter than 'not made from wine'. The 'Where opinions differ' line is accurate. no issues.
rows.method: 1 web search (seekersguidance.org search-result excerpt, shared with R1272); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Hanafi answer (Faraz Rabbani): paper then water is best; paper alone meets the sunnah while the filth stays at the exit; washing is required if it spreads beyond the exit and its immediate surround
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/what-is-the-best-way-to-clean-oneself-after-using-the-toilet/: 'It is optimal to first use tissue paper or the like until one cleans the area, and to then wash it with water ... if the filth goes beyond the place of exit and its immediately surrounding area, then one must wash. Wiping alone will not be enough.'

claims.claim: Yusuf Weltch: toilet paper alone fulfils the basic sunnah; washing is better
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity/is-cleaning-myself-with-toilet-paper-in-the-bathroom-sufficient/: 'the sunna will be achieved by wiping, even though washing is better and recommended when possible.'

claims.claim: Ilyas Patel: after cleaning properly, ignore doubts
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity/what-can-i-do-if-i-have-misgivings-after-istinja/: 'ignore the doubt afterward, as it is only a misgiving'; suffice with the sunna method of removing filth.

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 262a (Salman): the Prophet forbade facing the qibla, cleaning with the right hand, fewer than three stones, and dung or bone
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search-result excerpt), https://sunnah.com/muslim:262b (same hadith as 262a): a polytheist joked that the Prophet 'teaches you even about your excrement'; Salman said he commanded them not to face the qibla, not to cleanse with the right hand and not to use fewer than three stones, none of them dung or bone.

rows.notes: All four sources match the site's wording. The left-hand instruction rests on Muslim 262. The note that the schools differ on facing the qibla in a washroom inside a building is the standard picture (Hanafi stricter, others allow it indoors with a screen) and was not searched. no issues.
rows.method: 2 web searches (seekersguidance.org for the three answers; sunnah.com for Muslim 262); direct page opening was not available

claims.claim: Hanafi answer (Tabraze Azam): at least a quarter of the head itself must be wiped; wiping over the scarf does not count
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/can-i-wipe-my-headscarf-instead-of-my-head-in-wudu/: it is obligatory to wipe one quarter of the head, and wiping the headscarf or turban 'doesn't fulfill the obligation, derived from the decisive Qur'anic text, of wiping the head, and is thus problematic, and practically, invalid.'

claims.claim: Hanbali school allows wiping over a scarf wrapped under the chin; one may follow the Hanbali view if both wudu and prayer are valid in that school (Ilyas Patel)
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search-result excerpt), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/adab/how-can-a-working-woman-always-be-in-wudu/: 'In the Hanbali school, it is permissible to wipe over the turban ... and allowed for women to wipe over their scarves so long as it's wrapped under the chin'; 'One can follow another school, in this case, the Hanbali school in wudu, ensuring both wudu and prayer are valid in another school for it to be legally valid.'

claims.claim: Conditions: the scarf was put on while in wudu, for one day and night (three when travelling)
claims.evidence: Not visible in any search-result excerpt; these are the standard Hanbali conditions for wiping over a turban or khimar, the same as for leather socks (from standard references, not confirmed online).

rows.notes: Both SeekersGuidance answers say what the site says; only the duration and 'worn in wudu' conditions were not in a search-result excerpt. Naming rule: the read-more label 'Wudu and ghusl guide' leads with Arabic; the nav calls the page 'Washing before prayer (wudu and ghusl)'. The site's admission that Shafi'i and Maliki sources were not checked is honest; both schools would not accept wiping the scarf alone.
rows.method: 2 web searches (seekersguidance.org for both answers, second one for the Hanbali conditions); direct page opening was not available
